n: Abraham is now very old, and the Lord has blessed him in everything. One task remains: finding a covenant wife for Isaac so the promises can continue.

f.g: Very old.

n: Abraham calls his senior servant, the manager of his household, and has him place his hand under Abraham’s thigh—a solemn way of taking an oath in that culture.

f.g: Senior or chief servant; often thought to be Eliezer (15:2), though he is unnamed here.

f.w: Put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh
f.g: An oath gesture near the source of life, perhaps invoking the covenant and posterity.

n: The servant must swear by the Lord not to choose a Canaanite wife for Isaac. Marrying within the covenant would preserve faith in the true God.

f.w: the God of heaven, and the God of the earth
f.g: God rules over all—not just a local deity.

f.w: not take a wife unto my son of the daughters of the Canaanites

n: Instead, he must go back to Abraham’s relatives in Mesopotamia, who shared family ties and at least some knowledge of the Lord.

f.g: The region of Haran in northern Mesopotamia.

n: The servant raises a practical concern: what if the woman refuses to come? Should Isaac move back there?

f.g: Perhaps; what if.

n: Abraham firmly says no. Isaac must not leave the promised land.

f.w: bring not my son thither again
f.g: Isaac’s future is tied to Canaan, the land of promise.

n: Abraham expresses confident faith: the God who called him and promised the land will send an angel ahead to prepare the way.

f.w: he shall send his angel before thee

n: If the woman will not come, the servant will be free from the oath—but he must never take Isaac back there.

f.g: You will be released from the obligation.

n: The servant takes the oath as Abraham asked.

f.g: Took a solemn oath.

n: The servant sets out with ten camels loaded with gifts, traveling to the city of Nahor in Mesopotamia—a journey of several hundred miles.

f.g: Hebrew Aram-naharaim, “Aram of the two rivers,” in northern Mesopotamia.
Either Haran or a town named after Abraham’s brother Nahor.

n: He arrives at the town well in the evening, when women came to draw water—a natural place to meet the town’s young women.

f.g: Fetching water was a daily task often done by young women.

n: The servant prays for success and for God to show loyal kindness to Abraham. This is the first recorded prayer for guidance in the Bible.

f.g: Grant me success.
Hebrew ḥesed — covenant loyalty and love.

n: He describes the situation to the Lord: he stands at the well as the young women come out.

f.w: the daughters of the men of the city
f.g: The young women of the town.

n: He asks for a specific sign: the right woman will offer water not only to him but to his camels. That would reveal generosity and a willing heart—a camel can drink many gallons.

f.w: I will give thy camels drink also
f.g: Watering ten thirsty camels was hard work—a sign of exceptional kindness.
Chosen; designated.

n: Before he has finished praying, Rebekah arrives—and she is Abraham’s own relative. God answers even as the prayer is offered.
Rebekah is beautiful and unmarried. She goes down to the spring and fills her jar.

f.g: Perhaps a spring reached by steps.

n: The servant runs to meet her and asks for a little water.

f.g: His eagerness shows he sees God’s hand at work.

n: Rebekah responds quickly and respectfully, lowering her jar to give him a drink.

f.g: Rebekah acts promptly—a recurring trait in this chapter.

n: Without being asked, she offers to water all his camels until they are satisfied—exactly the sign he prayed for.

f.g: Ten camels could drink well over a hundred gallons.

n: Rebekah runs back and forth, emptying her jar into the trough and drawing more, until all the camels have had enough.

f.g: A drinking basin for animals.

n: The servant watches silently, wondering whether this is truly the Lord’s answer.

f.g: Remained silent.
To know; to find out.

n: When the camels finish, he gives her a gold nose ring and two heavy gold bracelets—signs of Abraham’s wealth and the seriousness of his mission.

f.g: A nose ring (see verse 47).
About 4 ounces (115 grams) of gold.

n: He asks whose daughter she is and whether there is room to stay the night.

f.g: Spend the night.

n: Rebekah names her father and grandparents—Abraham’s relatives. The servant’s prayer is fully answered.
She adds that there is plenty of straw, feed, and room. Her hospitality matches Abraham’s.

f.g: Animal feed.

n: The servant bows and worships the Lord. Gratitude is his first response to answered prayer.
He praises the Lord for His steadfast kindness and faithfulness. “I being in the way, the LORD led me” is a lovely model: keep moving in faith, and God guides.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed and ’emet — loyal love and faithfulness, a frequent pair in scripture.

f.w: I being in the way, the LORD led me

n: Rebekah runs home and tells her mother’s household everything.

f.g: The women’s quarters of the household.

n: Her brother Laban runs out to the well to meet the man. Laban will play a big role in Jacob’s story later.

f.g: Means “white.”

n: Laban’s interest is sparked when he sees the gold jewelry. The narrator hints at Laban’s love of wealth, which shows again in Jacob’s day.

f.w: when he saw the earring and bracelets

n: Laban warmly welcomes the servant as one “blessed of the LORD,” saying the house and stable are ready.

f.g: Laban uses the name of the Lord, showing the family knew of Him.

n: The servant is welcomed in. The camels are unloaded and fed, and water is brought to wash the travelers’ feet.

f.g: Unloaded; unharnessed.

n: Food is served, but the servant refuses to eat until he explains his errand. Duty comes before comfort.

f.g: Food.
Mission; business.

n: He introduces himself simply as Abraham’s servant. He never gives his own name—his identity is in serving his master.

f.g: The servant remains unnamed throughout the chapter.

n: He tells how the Lord has made Abraham wealthy—essentially presenting Isaac’s family as a good match.

f.w: the LORD hath blessed my master greatly

n: Sarah bore a son in her old age, and Abraham has given him everything. Isaac is the sole heir.

f.w: unto him hath he given all that he hath

n: He explains the oath: Isaac must not marry a Canaanite.
He must find a wife from Abraham’s own family.

f.g: Abraham’s family clan.

n: He recounts his own question: what if the woman will not come?

f.w: Peradventure the woman will not follow me

n: He repeats Abraham’s faith that an angel would guide him. Retelling the story lets the family see God’s hand at every step.

f.g: Whom I serve and live in obedience to.

n: He explains that he would be freed from the oath if the family refused.
He describes arriving at the well and praying to Abraham’s God for success.

f.w: if now thou do prosper my way
f.g: If you will now make my journey succeed.

n: He repeats the sign he asked for: a young woman who would offer him water.

f.g: Here, the young unmarried woman.

n: …and who would also offer to water his camels. That woman would be the Lord’s choice.

f.g: Chosen; marked out.

n: He tells how Rebekah appeared even before he finished praying silently in his heart.

f.g: He had prayed silently—God hears unspoken prayers.

n: Rebekah did exactly what he had asked of the Lord.

f.g: Hurried.

n: He describes asking about her family and giving her the jewelry.

f.g: A nose ring.

n: He bowed and worshipped the Lord, who led him to his master’s relative. His account gives God all the credit.

f.w: led me in the right way

n: He asks for a clear answer: will the family deal kindly and truly with Abraham? Either way, he needs to know where to go next.

f.g: Show loyal kindness and faithfulness—echoing verse 27.

f.w: turn to the right hand, or to the left
f.g: Decide on his next move.

n: Laban and Bethuel recognize the matter comes from the Lord. They cannot argue with it.

f.w: we cannot speak unto thee bad or good
f.g: We cannot say anything one way or the other.

n: They agree: Rebekah may go to become Isaac’s wife, as the Lord has directed.

f.g: They accept the outcome as God’s will.

n: The servant bows to the ground in worship again. Each step of the journey is marked by gratitude.

f.g: A posture of deep reverence.

n: He gives Rebekah jewelry and clothing, and gifts to her brother and mother—customary betrothal gifts.

f.g: Clothing.
Valuable gifts, perhaps part of a bride-price.

n: After a night of feasting, the servant asks to leave right away.

f.g: Stayed.

n: Rebekah’s brother and mother ask for some time—at least ten days—before she leaves.

f.w: a few days, at the least ten
f.g: Possibly “days or ten,” a vague period, perhaps much longer.

n: The servant asks them not to delay him, since the Lord has made the journey succeed.

f.g: Don’t hold me back.

n: The family decides to let Rebekah decide for herself.

f.g: Ask her directly.

n: Rebekah answers simply: “I will go.” Like Abraham before her, she leaves home and family by faith for a land she has never seen.
They send Rebekah off with her nurse, Abraham’s servant, and his men.

f.g: Deborah, who later dies near Bethel (35:8).

n: Her family blesses her to become the mother of countless descendants who will overcome their enemies—remarkably echoing God’s promise to Abraham.

f.g: Literally “thousands of ten thousands”—a vast number.

f.w: possess the gate of those which hate them

n: Rebekah and her maids mount the camels and follow the servant home.

f.g: Her young female attendants.

n: Meanwhile Isaac has come from Beer-lahai-roi, where he lives in the Negev.

f.g: The well where God appeared to Hagar.

n: Isaac goes out in the evening to meditate in the field. As he looks up, he sees the camels approaching.

f.g: The Hebrew is uncertain—perhaps to pray, ponder, or walk.
Evening.

n: Rebekah looks up, sees Isaac, and quickly gets down from her camel.

f.g: Got down from; dismounted.

n: Learning the man is Isaac, she covers herself with a veil, as a bride customarily did.

f.g: A bride wore a veil before the wedding (compare 29:23-25).

n: The servant tells Isaac everything that happened—another testimony of God’s guidance.

f.g: The servant’s report completes his faithful mission.

n: Isaac brings Rebekah into Sarah’s tent, marries her, and loves her. Isaac is comforted after his mother’s death. This is the first time the Bible says a husband loved his wife.

f.g: The first mention of a husband’s love for his wife in scripture.
